question: The Tolkappiyam, the oldest surviving work of Tamil literature, was written by whom?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Tolkappiyar.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Tolkappiyar, a disciple of the sage Agasthya, composed the Tolkappiyam, the oldest available work in Tamil literature (तोलकाप्पियम् — तमिल का सबसे प्राचीन ग्रंथ)

 

• Strictly it is a treatise on Tamil grammar, but it also reveals the political and socio-economic conditions of the Sangam period, which makes it a historical source.

 

• According to tradition it survived the loss of the works of the Second Sangam, so it is the only text of that academy that we still possess.

 

• The work is sometimes called the fifth Veda of Tamil Nadu, showing the reverence it enjoyed.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sangam literature is dated roughly to about 2300 years ago, between the 3rd century BC and the 3rd century AD.

 

• Tamil tradition links Agasthya with the First and Second Sangams, and his pupil Tolkappiyar presided at the Second.

 

• Grammar books (Tolkappiyam) and anthologies (Ettutogai, Pattuppattu) are the main categories of Sangam texts.

 

• The Tolkappiyam is divided into three parts, dealing with letters, words and subject matter, and it is the earliest text to describe the Tamil poetic tradition.

 

NOTE

 

• Tiruvalluvar (Option 1): Tiruvalluvar is the author of the Tirukkural, a work on ethics and polity, which is included among the later Pathinenkilkanakku collection. He is not the author of the grammar text asked about here.

 

• Sittalai Sattanar (Option 2): Sittalai Sattanar wrote the epic Manimegalai, a Buddhist-flavoured Tamil narrative that continues the Silappadikaram story. It is an epic, not a grammar treatise, and it is not the oldest work.

 

• Nakkirar (Option 4): Nakkirar is remembered as the chairman of the Third Sangam at Madurai and as a famous poet of that assembly. He presided over an academy but is not credited with the Tolkappiyam.

question: Elango Adigal, the author of the Tamil epic Silappadikaram, was the brother of which ruler?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Cheran Senguttuvan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Elango Adigal, who composed the Silappadikaram, is described in tradition as the younger brother of the Chera king Cheran Senguttuvan (चेरन सेंगुट्टुवन — इलांगो आदिगल के भाई)

 

• Senguttuvan belonged to the Chera dynasty, which ruled parts of present-day Kerala from the capital Vanji.

 

• The epic narrates the story of Kovalan, Madhavi and Kannagi, and the Chera king is a central figure in its final section.

 

• Because the author belonged to a royal family and became a Jain monk (adigal), the epic gives a rare insider view of three Tamil kingdoms.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Senguttuvan is placed in the 2nd century AD and is best known for his expedition to the Himalayas.

 

• The Silappadikaram is one of the two great Tamil epics, the other being the Manimegalai.

 

• The emblem of the Chera kings was the bow.

 

• The epic is divided into three books named after the cities Puhar, Madurai and Vanji, which correspond to the Chola, Pandya and Chera kingdoms.

 

NOTE

 

• Karikala (Option 1): Karikala was a famous Sangam Chola ruler who is credited with founding the port city of Puhar. He belonged to the Chola line, so he cannot be the Chera brother of the epic's author.

 

• Nedunjeliyan Pandya (Option 3): Nedunjeliyan was a Pandya ruler of Madurai whose reign is linked in the epic with Kannagi's anger over Kovalan's death. He appears in the story but is not the author's brother.

 

• Rajaraja I (Option 4): Rajaraja I was an Imperial Chola king who ruled from 985 to 1014 AD and built the Brihadeshwara temple. He lived about eight centuries after the epic was composed and has no link with its author.

question: Which of the following Tamil epics was composed by Sittalai Sattanar?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Manimegalai.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sittalai Sattanar wrote the epic Manimegalai, which follows the life of Manimegalai, the daughter of Kovalan and Madhavi (मणिमेखलै — सित्तलै सत्तनार की रचना)

 

• The story continues the plot of the Silappadikaram, so the two together are called the twin epics of Tamil literature.

 

• Manimegalai is strongly influenced by Buddhism, as the heroine renounces the world to become a Buddhist nun.

 

• Along with the Silappadikaram it forms the two epics counted within the Sangam-age corpus in the class notes.

 

• Manimegalai and Silappadikaram are usually studied as a pair, because the second epic carries forward the lives of the characters introduced in the first.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Manimegalai gives useful descriptions of the port city of Puhar and its trading life.

 

• Silappadikaram has a Jain background, while Manimegalai has a Buddhist one.

 

• The pair of epics are also valuable for understanding society in early Tamilakam.

 

• The epic tells how the heroine gives up worldly life and follows Buddhist teaching, which shows that Buddhism had spread in the Tamil country.

 

NOTE

 

• Silappadikaram (Option 2): Silappadikaram was written by Elango Adigal, the brother of Cheran Senguttuvan, and tells the tale of Kovalan, Madhavi and Kannagi. It is the first epic, not the work of Sittalai Sattanar.

 

• Tolkappiyam (Option 3): Tolkappiyam is a grammar book by Tolkappiyar and is the oldest surviving Tamil work. It is not an epic, and it belongs to an earlier layer than the two epics.

 

• Pattuppattu (Option 4): Pattuppattu is the anthology of ten long poems that forms one of the main Sangam collections. It is a group of poems by many poets, not a single epic by Sittalai Sattanar.

question: Kovalan, Madhavi and Kannagi are the main characters of which Tamil work?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Silappadikaram.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Silappadikaram by Elango Adigal narrates the story of Kovalan, Madhavi and Kannagi, centred on a merchant, a dancer and a faithful wife (सिलप्पदिकारम् — कोवलन, माधवी और कण्णगी की कथा)

 

• Kovalan leaves his wife Kannagi for the dancer Madhavi, loses his wealth, and is unjustly executed at Madurai for allegedly stealing the queen's anklet.

 

• The title means 'the story of the anklet' (silambu), an object around which the whole tragedy turns.

 

• Kannagi later becomes a symbol of chastity and is worshipped as a goddess in Tamil tradition.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The epic is useful to historians because it describes the cities of Puhar, Madurai and Vanji.

 

• Chera king Senguttuvan is said to have brought a stone from the Himalayas to make an image of Kannagi.

 

• Its author Elango Adigal is believed to have been a Jain monk.

 

• Because the epic describes the fate of a merchant family of Puhar, it is also used as a source for the life of traders in the Sangam age.

 

NOTE

 

• Manimegalai (Option 1): Manimegalai is the sequel written by Sittalai Sattanar and focuses on the daughter of Kovalan and Madhavi. Kannagi is not its heroine, so it is not the main source of this story.

 

• Tolkappiyam (Option 2): Tolkappiyam is a work on grammar and does not tell any story of merchants or dancers. It is the oldest surviving Tamil text and deals with language rules and early society.

 

• Ettutogai (Option 4): Ettutogai is the 'Eight Anthologies' of short Sangam poems on love and war. It is a collection of verses by various poets and has no continuous plot about Kovalan.

question: According to Tamil tradition, who was the chairman of the Third Sangam at Madurai?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Nakkirar.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Third Sangam at Madurai was presided over by the poet Nakkirar, and many poets produced a large body of literature there, though only a few works survived (नक्कीरर — तृतीय संगम के अध्यक्ष)

 

• Tamil legends speak of three Sangams, or academies of poets, collectively called the Muchchangam.

 

• All three academies are said to have enjoyed the patronage of the Pandya kings.

 

• The first two Sangams belong largely to legend, while the third is linked with the surviving Sangam literature.

 

• The legends gave the academies a long mythical history, but modern historians treat the Third Sangam period as the real age of the surviving Tamil poems.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The First Sangam was held at the 'Then Madurai' under Agasthya, and no work from it survives.

 

• The Second Sangam was held at Kapadapuram under Agasthya and Tolkappiyar, and only the Tolkappiyam survives.

 

• The Third Sangam's surviving works include Ettutogai and Pattuppattu.

 

• Cheran Senguttuvan, Karikala and the Pandya kings are among the rulers praised by the poets who are supposed to have belonged to the third academy.

 

NOTE

 

• Agasthya (Option 2): Agasthya is the legendary sage who headed the First Sangam and, with his disciple, the Second. He did not preside over the Third Sangam at Madurai.

 

• Tolkappiyar (Option 3): Tolkappiyar was the disciple of Agasthya who shared the leadership of the Second Sangam and wrote the Tolkappiyam. He is linked to an earlier academy, not the Third.

 

• Mudathirumaran (Option 4): Mudathirumaran is named in the notes as the founder of the Third Sangam rather than its chairman. The question asks for the chairman, who was the poet Nakkirar.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Sangams:

1. Tamil legends speak of three Sangams, together called the Muchchangam.

2. All three enjoyed the royal patronage of the Pandyas.

3. Every work of the Second Sangam survives today.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The right choice is only 1 and 2: legend speaks of three Sangams (the Muchchangam) and all enjoyed Pandya patronage (संगम — तमिल कवियों की तीन सभाएँ, पांड्य संरक्षण)

 

• The third claim fails since nearly every literary work of the Second Sangam perished, with the Tolkappiyam the only exception.

 

• The Sangams are described as academies of Tamil poets held at Madurai and nearby places such as Kapadapuram.

 

• The First Sangam has no surviving work at all, so only the Third Sangam preserved a real body of literature.

 

• The distinction between lost and surviving literature is the usual SSC trap, since only a fraction of Sangam writing has come down to us.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The word Sangam means a gathering or assembly of poets and scholars.

 

• The Pandyas' capital Madurai was the centre of the Sangam tradition.

 

• The Sangam period is generally dated between the 3rd century BC and the 3rd century AD.

 

• The traditional claim that the Sangams lasted for thousands of years is treated as legend, but the third academy corresponds to real poems of the early centuries.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): Only 2 and 3 wrongly accepts statement 3, which claims that the Second Sangam's works survive. In fact only Tolkappiyam from that academy remains, so statement 3 cannot be part of the correct answer.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): Only 1 and 3 carries the false statement 3 and drops the correct statement 2. The Pandyas patronised all the three academies, so the answer must contain statement 2.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): 1, 2 and 3 is wrong because statement 3 is false. The Second Sangam lost all its literature except the Tolkappiyam, so accepting all three statements overstates what has survived.

question:
Match the Sangam-age dynasty with its royal emblem.

a. Cheras

b. Cholas

c. Pandyas

i. Carp (fish)

ii. Bow

iii. Tiger
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct matching is Cheras - Bow, Cholas - Tiger, Pandyas - Carp (fish) (चेर — धनुष, चोल — बाघ, पांड्य — कार्प मछली)

 

• These emblems appeared on the coins and banners of the three dynasties that ruled the Tamil country in the Sangam age.

 

• The Cheras ruled parts of modern Kerala, the Cholas the Kaveri region, and the Pandyas the far south of Tamil Nadu.

 

• The tiger emblem continued with the Cholas of the imperial age, who used it on their seals and coins.

 

• The emblems were not decorative alone, because Sangam poems and later records mention them on banners, seals and coins of the three crowned kings.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Capitals: Cheras - Vanji, Cholas - Uraiyur and later Puhar, Pandyas - Madurai.

 

• The three kingdoms together are known in Sangam texts as the Muventar (three crowned kings).

 

• Pandya coins and Sangam poems both mention the fish emblem.

 

• Later Chola rulers continued the use of the tiger emblem on their coins and copper plate seals, which shows its importance to the dynasty.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iii, b-ii, c-i (Option 1): a-iii, b-ii, c-i gives the Cheras the tiger and the Cholas the bow. This swaps the two emblems, since the tiger belonged to the Cholas and the bow to the Cheras.

 

• a-i, b-iii, c-ii (Option 3): a-i, b-iii, c-ii gives the Cheras the carp and the Pandyas the bow. The carp was the Pandya emblem and the bow the Chera one, so two pairs are wrong.

 

• a-ii, b-i, c-iii (Option 4): a-ii, b-i, c-iii pairs the Cholas with the carp and the Pandyas with the tiger. Both are wrong because the Cholas had the tiger and the Pandyas the fish.

question:
Match the dynasty with its capital.

a. Cheras

b. Pandyas

c. Early Cholas

d. Imperial Chola Rajendra I

i. Madurai

ii. Vanji

iii. Uraiyur

iv. Gangaikondacholapuram
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct match is Cheras - Vanji, Pandyas - Madurai, Early Cholas - Uraiyur, Rajendra I - Gangaikondacholapuram (वंजि, मदुरै, उरैयूर, गंगैकोंडचोलपुरम)

 

• Vanji was the Chera seat in present-day Kerala, and Madurai was the Pandya capital and home of the Sangam academies.

 

• The Sangam Cholas ruled first from Uraiyur and later shifted to Puhar (Kaveripattinam).

 

• Rajendra I founded Gangaikondacholapuram after his northern campaign and made it his capital.

 

• The two Chola capitals in the list belong to different ages, so the list also shows how political centres moved from the Sangam age to the imperial age.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Puhar was also the main Chola port, known as Kaveripattinam.

 

• Vanji is identified by many scholars with Karur, as one SSC question has accepted.

 

• Gangaikondacholapuram has a Siva temple built by Rajendra I.

 

• Gangaikondacholapuram remained the Chola capital for several generations after Rajendra I before the dynasty returned to its old centres.

 

NOTE

 

• a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv (Option 1): a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv swaps the Chera and Pandya capitals. Madurai was the Pandya seat of power, while Vanji served the Cheras, so the first two pairs are wrong.

 

• a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv (Option 2): a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv swaps the Pandya and early Chola capitals. Uraiyur was the early Chola seat and Madurai the Pandya one, so the middle pairs are incorrect.

 

• a-iv, b-i, c-iii, d-ii (Option 4): a-iv, b-i, c-iii, d-ii joins the Cheras to Gangaikondacholapuram and Rajendra I to Vanji. That mixes up a Sangam-age capital with an Imperial Chola one, and is chronologically impossible.

question: Vanji, the capital of the Cheras, is identified with present-day Karur in Tamil Nadu. Vanji was the capital of which dynasty?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Cheras.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Vanji was the capital of the Cheras, who ruled parts of modern Kerala in the Sangam age (वंजि — चेर राजवंश की राजधानी)

 

• The Chera royal emblem was the bow, and one of their best-known kings was Cheran Senguttuvan.

 

• Senguttuvan's brother Elango Adigal wrote the Silappadikaram, in which Vanji figures prominently.

 

• Vanji's location is debated, but the SSC key treats it as the Chera capital without ambiguity.

 

• A question on capitals is best answered by pairing each dynasty with its region: Cheras in the west, Pandyas in the far south and Cholas in the Kaveri basin.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas formed the three crowned kingdoms of the early Tamil country.

 

• Senguttuvan belongs to the 2nd century AD.

 

• Chera territory lay on the western side of the peninsula, in what is now Kerala.

 

• The Chera country was famous for pepper, which attracted Roman traders to ports such as Muziris, and this trade enriched the kingdom.

 

NOTE

 

• Pandyas (Option 1): The Pandyas had their capital at Madurai in the extreme south of Tamil Nadu and used the carp as their emblem. Madurai, not Vanji, was their seat, so this option is wrong.

 

• Cholas (Option 2): The Cholas ruled from Uraiyur and later from Puhar in the Kaveri region and used a tiger emblem. Vanji was never their capital, so this cannot be the answer.

 

• Pallavas (Option 3): The Pallavas ruled from Kanchipuram and were a later dynasty, not one of the three Sangam-age kingdoms. Vanji has no association with them, which rules this option out.

question: Which Sangam-age Chera king is especially remembered for his military expedition to the Himalayas?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Cheran Senguttuvan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Cheran Senguttuvan (2nd century AD) is the Chera king whose expedition to the Himalayas stands out among his achievements; he defeated several north Indian rulers (चेरन सेंगुट्टुवन — हिमालय अभियान)

 

• His campaign is celebrated in Tamil tradition, and the Himalayan stone was reportedly used for the Kannagi image.

 

• He belonged to the Chera dynasty, whose capital was Vanji and whose emblem was the bow.

 

• He was the brother of Elango Adigal, the poet of the Silappadikaram.

 

• The northern expedition shows that the Tamil kings of the age were aware of the politics of the north, even though they kept their own culture distinct.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Silappadikaram is a key literary source for his reign.

 

• The Himalayan campaign shows the contact between the Tamil south and the north in the Sangam age.

 

• Chera rule in Kerala later declined and revived in the early medieval period.

 

• Senguttuvan's reign is dated to the 2nd century AD, and his story shows the links between Sangam literature and later epic traditions.

 

NOTE

 

• Karikala (Option 1): Karikala was a Sangam Chola who is credited with founding Puhar and is linked with water works on the Kaveri. His reputation rests on port building and irrigation, not a Himalayan campaign.

 

• Neduncheliyan (Option 3): Neduncheliyan was a Pandya king of Madurai known from Sangam poems and the Silappadikaram story. He was a southern ruler and is not credited with the Himalayan expedition.

 

• Mudathirumaran (Option 4): Mudathirumaran, according to the notes, founded the Third Sangam, so he is associated with literary patronage. He is not described as a Chera king or a conqueror of the Himalayas.

question: Karikala, a famous king of the Sangam Cholas, is credited with founding which port city?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Puhar.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Karikala founded the port city of Puhar (Kaveripattinam) on the Kaveri delta, and it became a major Chola centre of trade (पुहार — करिकाल द्वारा स्थापित बंदरगाह नगर)

 

• He ranks as the most famous of the Sangam Cholas, whose emblem was the tiger and whose first capital was Uraiyur.

 

• Puhar later served as the Chola capital as well, since the capital shifted there from Uraiyur.

 

• Sangam poems such as the Pattinappalai describe Puhar and its overseas commerce.

 

• The foundation of a port by a Chola king reflects the importance of overseas trade for the Kaveri delta economy in the Sangam age.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Karikala is also traditionally credited with the Kallanai (Grand Anicut) on the Kaveri, one of the oldest water-regulation structures still in use.

 

• Puhar is the same city as Kaveripattinam.

 

• The Silappadikaram begins with Kovalan's life at Puhar.

 

• Roman gold coins found in southern India show that the ports of the Tamil country were part of a wide trading network in the early centuries AD.

 

NOTE

 

• Korkai (Option 1): Korkai was the early port of the Pandyas on the south-east coast, famed for pearl fisheries. It served the Pandya kingdom and was not established by the Chola king Karikala.

 

• Muziris (Option 2): Muziris was a leading Chera port on the Malabar coast known for the pepper trade with the Romans. It lay on the west coast in Chera country, far from Karikala's Chola domain.

 

• Mamallapuram (Option 3): Mamallapuram was developed by the Pallava kings, especially Narasimhavarman I, as a port and temple site in the 7th century AD. It is much later than Karikala and belongs to a different dynasty.

question: Kaveripattinam, the main Chola port, is also known by which name?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Puhar.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Kaveripattinam was the principal port of the Cholas and is also known as Puhar (कावेरीपट्टनम् — पुहार, चोलों का प्रमुख बंदरगाह)

 

• The city stood at the mouth of the Kaveri river and was the gateway for Chola overseas trade.

 

• According to the notes, Karikala founded Puhar, and the Chola capital moved there from Uraiyur.

 

• It is a major setting of the epic Silappadikaram, where Kovalan and Kannagi begin their life.

 

• The use of two names for one city is common in the Tamil country, where Sangam-age names often differ from the later medieval ones.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Pandya port of Korkai was famous for pearls.

 

• Chera trade centred on Muziris on the Malabar coast.

 

• Puhar's fame comes from Sangam poetry and the accounts of foreign traders.

 

• Puhar is also said to have been damaged by the sea in later times, which explains why its remains are now partly under water.

 

NOTE

 

• Korkai (Option 1): Korkai was the early Pandya port near the mouth of the Tambraparni, associated with pearl fishery. It belongs to the southern kingdom, so it cannot be the other name of the Chola port.

 

• Tondi (Option 3): Tondi was a Chera-associated port on the western side of the peninsula in Sangam poems. It is not a name for the Kaveri-mouth port and has no link with the Cholas.

 

• Arikamedu (Option 4): Arikamedu near Pondicherry is an archaeological site where Roman pottery was found, showing Indo-Roman trade. It is an east-coast trading station, but it is not another name of Kaveripattinam.

question: In the Sangam age, the Chola capital was first located at ______ and later shifted to ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Uraiyur; Puhar.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The early Cholas ruled first from Uraiyur (near modern Tiruchi) and later moved the capital to Puhar (Kaveripattinam) (उरैयूर से पुहार — चोल राजधानी का स्थानांतरण)

 

• The Chola kingdom of this period stretched from the Tiruchi region down to southern Andhra Pradesh, as the notes record.

 

• Karikala, the best-known Sangam Chola, founded the port city of Puhar and strengthened it.

 

• The Chola royal emblem in this period was the tiger.

 

• The shift of the Chola capital to the coast reflects the growing role of maritime trade and the strength of port revenue in early Tamilakam.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Imperial Cholas of the 9th century later moved the centre to Thanjavur and Gangaikondacholapuram.

 

• Uraiyur was famous for cotton cloth in ancient times.

 

• Do not confuse the early and imperial capitals: Uraiyur-Puhar belong to the Sangam age.

 

• Uraiyur, the first Chola capital, lies near modern Tiruchirappalli and was well known in the ancient world as a centre of cotton textiles.

 

NOTE

 

• Madurai; Puhar (Option 2): Madurai was the Pandya capital and the seat of the Sangams, not the first seat of the Cholas. The pairing therefore begins with the wrong kingdom's capital.

 

• Vanji; Uraiyur (Option 3): Vanji was the Chera capital in Kerala, so it cannot be the first Chola capital. The sequence is also reversed because Uraiyur came before Puhar for the Cholas.

 

• Puhar; Thanjavur (Option 4): Thanjavur became the Chola centre only with the Imperial Cholas from the 9th century, about six hundred years after Sangam times. Puhar was not the first Chola capital either, so this pair is wrong.

question: Which of the following was NOT one of the three major dynasties that ruled the Tamil country in the Sangam age?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Pallavas.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The three Sangam-age dynasties were the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas; the Pallavas were not among them (पल्लव — संगमकालीन तीन राज्यों में शामिल नहीं)

 

• The Pallavas rose later and ruled from Kanchipuram, becoming prominent from about the 6th century AD.

 

• The three Sangam kingdoms are listed in the notes with their regions, capitals and emblems: bow, tiger and carp.

 

• Vijayalaya of the Imperial Chola line is believed to have been a feudatory of the Pallavas, which shows the Pallavas as a later overlord.

 

• The Pallavas, by contrast, became a major power only after the Sangam age, which makes them the natural exception whenever the list names the Sangam dynasties.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Mahendravarman I and Narasimhavarman I were Pallava rulers (covered in the next chapter).

 

• Pallava art includes the Shore Temple and Seven Rathas at Mamallapuram.

 

• The Sangam kingdoms are referred to together as the Muventar.

 

• The Pallava kings are remembered for the Shore Temple, the Seven Rathas and the rock-cut caves of Mamallapuram, which belong to a later period.

 

NOTE

 

• Cheras (Option 1): The Cheras ruled the Kerala region from Vanji and used the bow emblem. They were certainly one of the three Sangam powers, so they do not fit this NOT-type question.

 

• Pandyas (Option 3): The Pandyas ruled the southern Tamil country from Madurai and patronised the Sangams, with the carp as their emblem. They were a Sangam-age dynasty, so they cannot be the exception.

 

• Cholas (Option 4): The Cholas ruled from Uraiyur and later Puhar, with the tiger as emblem, and produced Karikala. They were a core Sangam kingdom, so they cannot be the odd one out.

question:
Consider the following statements about Karikala:

1. He was a famous king of the Sangam Cholas.

2. He founded the port city of Puhar.

3. He belonged to the Pandya dynasty of Madurai.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Only the first two claims hold: Karikala was a famous Sangam Chola king and founded the port city of Puhar (करिकाल — संगमकालीन चोल शासक)

 

• Statement 3 fails because Karikala was a Chola, not a Pandya; the Pandya capital was Madurai and their emblem the carp.

 

• As a Chola, his dynasty used the tiger emblem and had Uraiyur as the early capital.

 

• An SSC key also states that Karikala belonged to the Chola dynasty and is remembered for constructing the Grand Anicut (Kallanai).

 

• Karikala is one of the best-known names of the early Tamil country and appears frequently in Sangam poems such as the Pattinappalai.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Kallanai on the Kaveri is built of stone and is still used for irrigation.

 

• Puhar's merchants traded with Rome and Southeast Asia.

 

• Do not mix Karikala (Sangam Chola) with Rajaraja I (Imperial Chola).

 

• The Kallanai, built across the Kaveri, is often quoted as the oldest functioning dam in India, and it is attributed by tradition to Karikala.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): Only 2 and 3 treats Karikala as a Pandya, which is wrong. Statement 1 is true as well, so dropping it makes this option incomplete and inaccurate.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): Only 1 and 3 accepts the Pandya claim in statement 3 and ignores statement 2. Karikala did found Puhar and was a Chola, so this combination misreads both facts.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): 1, 2 and 3 would be right only if statement 3 were true, but Karikala was a Chola king of the Kaveri region. The false third claim spoils the whole combination.

question:
Consider the following statements about Cheran Senguttuvan:

1. He belonged to the 2nd century AD.

2. His expedition to the Himalayas is among his best-known achievements.

3. He ruled from Madurai.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The first two claims are accurate: Senguttuvan is placed in the 2nd century AD and his Himalayan expedition stands out among his military achievements (सेंगुट्टुवन — द्वितीय शताब्दी, हिमालय अभियान)

 

• Placing him at Madurai is an error because he was a Chera, whose capital was Vanji, while Madurai was the Pandya capital.

 

• He is said to have defeated several north Indian monarchs during this campaign.

 

• His brother Elango Adigal composed the Silappadikaram in which he features.

 

• His connection with the epic makes him one of the few Sangam rulers for whom both literary and traditional evidence is available.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Chera emblem was the bow.

 

• Chera land covered parts of Kerala.

 

• Senguttuvan is often listed among the greatest Sangam-age kings along with Karikala.

 

• The Himalayan stone is said to have been bathed in the Ganga before it was carried south to make the image of Kannagi.

 

• Sangam poems also describe the Chera ports of Muziris and Tondi, where pepper and other spices were exchanged for Roman gold, enriching the kingdom.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): Only 2 and 3 contains the false claim that he ruled from Madurai. Madurai was the Pandya capital, so statement 3 cannot be accepted, and statement 1 is also true.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): Only 1 and 3 keeps the wrong statement 3 and leaves out the Himalayan expedition. The campaign is the chief reason he is remembered, so this combination is incomplete.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): 1, 2 and 3 fails because Senguttuvan was a Chera with his seat at Vanji. Placing him at Madurai confuses the Chera and Pandya kingdoms.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Pandyas of the Sangam age:

1. They ruled present-day southern Tamil Nadu.

2. Their capital was Madurai.

3. Their royal emblem was the carp (fish).
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• All three statements are correct: the Pandyas ruled southern Tamil Nadu from Madurai and had the carp as their emblem (पांड्य — मदुरै, मछली प्रतीक)

 

• Madurai was also the seat of the Sangam academies, which enjoyed Pandya royal patronage.

 

• The Pandya kingdom was one of the three crowned kingdoms of early Tamilakam alongside the Cholas and Cheras.

 

• Their fish emblem appears in Sangam poems and on their coins and flags.

 

• Sangam kings are described in poems as patrons of bards, who received gifts of gold, horses and elephants for praising the rulers in verse.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Pandya port Korkai was famous for pearls.

 

• The Pandyas later revived and in the 13th century ended Chola rule by defeating Rajendra III.

 

• The Pandyas used the fish emblem even in medieval times.

 

• Pandya kings in Sangam poems are said to have traded in pearls from the Gulf of Mannar, which made the kingdom wealthy and well known abroad.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 1): Only 1 and 2 omits the emblem statement. Statement 3 is accurate because the carp was the Pandya emblem, so excluding it makes the answer incomplete.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 3): Only 2 and 3 leaves out the regional statement. Statement 1 is accurate because the Pandyas did rule the southern part of Tamil Nadu, so this option is incomplete.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 4): Only 1 and 3 drops the capital statement. Statement 2 is accurate since Madurai was the Pandya capital, so the combination is incomplete.

question:
Assertion (A): The Tolkappiyam is useful to historians although it is basically a grammar book.

Reason (R): It also tells us about the political and socio-economic conditions of the Sangam period.
option_1: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_2: A is true but R is false
option_3: A is false but R is true
option_4: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion: the Tolkappiyam, though a grammar text, also describes the political and socio-economic conditions of the Sangam age (तोलकाप्पियम् — व्याकरण के साथ सामाजिक-आर्थिक जानकारी)

 

• Its author, Tolkappiyar, was a disciple of Agasthya and the Tolkappiyam is the oldest surviving Tamil literary work.

 

• Historians therefore use it together with the anthologies and epics to reconstruct early Tamil society.

 

• Its usefulness as a source follows directly from the social and political material in it, which is exactly what R states.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• It is also called the fifth Veda of Tamil Nadu in tradition.

 

• Sangam literature is about 2300 years old.

 

• Other sources include the Silappadikaram and the accounts of Greek and Roman traders.

 

• Another work of the period, the Tirukkural by Tiruvalluvar, is a famous text on ethics and is counted among the Pathinenkilkanakku.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 1): The option that says R is not the explanation is wrong, because the historical value of the book comes from the social and political details that R mentions. R directly explains A.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 2): The option that says A is true but R is false is wrong, since the Tolkappiyam does carry information about political and socio-economic life, as the notes say.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 3): The option that says A is false is wrong because the Tolkappiyam is indeed a book on grammar that historians consult. Both parts of the statement are true.

question: Which of the following is NOT a work of Sangam-age Tamil literature?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mrichchhakatika.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mrichchhakatika, a Sanskrit play attributed to Shudraka, is not a work of Sangam literature (मृच्छकटिकम् — संस्कृत नाटक, संगम साहित्य नहीं)

 

• Sangam literature is made up of Tamil works such as the Tolkappiyam, Ettutogai, Pattuppattu, Pathinenkilkanakku and the epics Silappadikaram and Manimegalai.

 

• The Sangam corpus dates to about 2300 years ago and was composed in Tamil in the south.

 

• Mrichchhakatika ('The Little Clay Cart') is a Sanskrit drama set in Ujjayini and belongs to northern classical Sanskrit literature.

 

• The question tests the habit of separating Tamil Sangam works from Sanskrit classics, which belong to a different linguistic and regional tradition.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sanskrit drama also includes the plays of Kalidasa and Bhasa.

 

• Pathinenkilkanakku (the 'Eighteen Minor Works') includes the Tirukkural.

 

• Eight collections (Ettutogai) and ten long poems (Pattuppattu) are two key anthology sets.

 

• Pathinenkilkanakku means the eighteen minor works, and these are mainly didactic poems, in contrast to the longer idylls and love poems of earlier collections.

 

NOTE

 

• Ettutogai (Option 1): Ettutogai is the 'Eight Anthologies' of Sangam poems and is explicitly listed in the notes. Since it is a genuine Sangam work, it cannot be the odd one out.

 

• Pattuppattu (Option 3): Pattuppattu, the 'Ten Idylls', is another major Sangam anthology named in the notes. It belongs to the same corpus and so does not answer a NOT-type question.

 

• Manimegalai (Option 4): Manimegalai is one of the two Sangam-age epics by Sittalai Sattanar, as the notes state. It is a Tamil work of the period, so it cannot be the exception.

question: The term 'Muchchangam' used in the notes on the Sangam Age refers to:
option_4: Three Sangams or Tamil literary academies together
solution_text:
The correct answer is Three Sangams or Tamil literary academies together.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Muchchangam refers to the three Sangams together, the legendary academies of Tamil poets that met at Madurai and elsewhere (मुच्चंगम — तीन संगमों का सामूहिक नाम)

 

• The three academies are the First Sangam (Then Madurai), the Second Sangam (Kapadapuram) and the Third Sangam (Madurai).

 

• All three are said to have enjoyed the royal patronage of the Pandyas.

 

• Literature survives mainly from the Third Sangam, whereas the first two are known mostly through legend, plus the Tolkappiyam from the Second.

 

• Because the three academies are described in legend, historians prefer to rely on the surviving poems rather than on the traditional lists of chairmen.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• 'Sangam' means a meeting or assembly of poets.

 

• Agasthya headed the first Sangam; Nakkirar headed the third.

 

• The Sangam period saw the writing of Ettutogai and Pattuppattu.

 

• The notes record that the Tolkappiyam is the only literary work of the second academy to have survived, which is why it is so important.

 

NOTE

 

• Three Chola kings (Option 1): Three Chola kings is wrong because the term concerns literary assemblies, not rulers. The Cholas were one of three dynasties, but the Muchchangam has nothing to do with their kings.

 

• Three ports of the Pandyas (Option 2): Three ports of the Pandyas is wrong, since the word is about poets' academies. Pandya ports such as Korkai exist, but none of them is called by this term.

 

• Three epics of Tamil literature (Option 3): Three epics of Tamil literature is wrong because there are two epics, the Silappadikaram and the Manimegalai. The term denotes three academies, not any set of books.

question: Who is regarded as the founder of the Imperial Chola line in the 9th century AD?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Vijayalaya.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Vijayalaya founded the Imperial Chola line in the 9th century AD, reviving Chola power after the Sangam age (विजयालय — शाही चोल वंश का संस्थापक)

 

• He is believed to have begun as a feudatory of the Pallavas before he established an independent kingdom in the Kaveri region.

 

• His capital is given in the notes as Thanjavur (Tanjore), which later became the heart of Chola power.

 

• From this base his successors expanded until the dynasty peaked under Rajaraja I and Rajendra I.

 

• The imperial line was different from the early Cholas because it had a stable administration, a strong army and the capacity to expand beyond the Kaveri basin.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Standard accounts say Vijayalaya captured Thanjavur from the Muttaraiyars and built a temple for the goddess Nishumbhasudini.

 

• The dynasty was ended in the 13th century when Rajendra III was defeated by the Pandyas.

 

• Do not confuse the Imperial Cholas with the Sangam Cholas of Karikala's age.

 

• The Imperial Chola line is separated from the Sangam Cholas by several centuries, during which the Pallavas and Pandyas were the main powers in the Tamil country.

 

NOTE

 

• Rajaraja I (Option 2): Rajaraja I (985-1014 AD) built the Brihadeshwara temple and took Chola power to a peak, but he was not the first of the imperial line. He belonged to a later generation than the founder.

 

• Rajendra I (Option 3): Rajendra I (1012-1044 AD) took the title Gangaikonda Chola after his northern campaign and founded a new capital. He was the son of Rajaraja I and many decades later than the founder.

 

• Karikala (Option 4): Karikala was a famous Sangam-age Chola who founded Puhar roughly seven centuries before the imperial dynasty began. He belongs to the early Chola line, not the imperial one.

question:
Consider the following statements about Vijayalaya:

1. He founded the Imperial Chola line.

2. He is believed to have been a feudatory of the Pallavas.

3. He built the Brihadeshwara temple at Tanjore.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The first two claims stand: Vijayalaya founded the Imperial Chola line and is believed to have started as a Pallava feudatory (विजयालय — पल्लवों का सामंत, शाही चोलों का संस्थापक)

 

• The third claim is false as the Brihadeshwara temple at Tanjore was built by Rajaraja I in 1010 AD, about a century and a half later.

 

• The founder's rise came in the 9th century when Pallava authority was weakening in the Tamil plain.

 

• Later Chola kings grew from a feudatory family into the greatest power in South India.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Imperial Chola line is conventionally dated from the 9th century.

 

• The Pallavas ruled from Kanchipuram.

 

• Rajaraja I's temple is also called the Rajarajeswara temple.

 

• The Pallavas, whose feudatory he is thought to have been, were eventually replaced by the Cholas as the dominant power in the Tamil region.

 

• After Vijayalaya the dynasty's early rulers included Aditya I and Parantaka I, who gradually extended Chola rule at the cost of the Pallavas and Pandyas.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): Only 2 and 3 contains the false claim that Vijayalaya built the Big Temple. The temple is the work of Rajaraja I, and statement 1 is also true, so this combination is wrong.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): Only 1 and 3 repeats the same wrong claim about the temple and ignores the Pallava link in statement 2. Because statement 3 is false, this option cannot be correct.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): 1, 2 and 3 would require Vijayalaya to be the builder of the Brihadeshwara temple. That temple was completed in 1010 AD under Rajaraja I, so including statement 3 is an error.

question: Chola power reached its highest point under which two rulers, according to the notes?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rajaraja I and Rajendra I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Chola power touched its highest point under Rajaraja I and his son Rajendra I (राजराज प्रथम और राजेंद्र प्रथम — चोल शक्ति का चरमोत्कर्ष)

 

• Rajaraja I ruled from 985 to 1014 AD and Rajendra I from 1012 to 1044 AD, so father and son together covered nearly sixty years of expansion.

 

• Their reigns saw conquests in Sri Lanka and the north, a strong navy, and the great temples at Thanjavur and Gangaikondacholapuram.

 

• A famous SSC key calls Rajaraja I the most powerful Chola ruler.

 

• Together the reigns of father and son cover the period in which the Chola navy, army and temple building all reached their greatest scale.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The two reigns overlapped briefly because Rajendra I was made co-ruler in 1012 AD.

 

• Rajendra I was the son of Rajaraja I.

 

• After them Chola power slowly declined until Rajendra III, the last ruler.

 

• Rajaraja I was succeeded by his son, who shifted the centre of the empire to a new city built after the northern campaign.

 

NOTE

 

• Vijayalaya and Parantaka I (Option 2): Vijayalaya founded the line, and Parantaka I, a later king, extended it, but the empire had not yet reached its peak then. Neither belongs to the pair associated with the greatest expansion.

 

• Kulottunga I and Rajendra III (Option 3): Kulottunga I came after the peak, and Rajendra III was the last Chola king who lost his realm to the Pandyas. The pair stands for the late and declining phase, not the climax.

 

• Karikala and Vijayalaya (Option 4): Karikala was a Sangam Chola and Vijayalaya the founder of the imperial line, so they are separated by about seven centuries. They cannot form the pair of peak-era rulers.

question: The Brihadeshwara temple at Tanjore, dedicated to Shiva, was built in 1010 AD by which ruler?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rajaraja I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Rajaraja I built the Brihadeshwara (Rajarajeswara) temple at Tanjore in 1010 AD, dedicated to Shiva (बृहदीश्वर मंदिर, तंजावुर — राजराज प्रथम)

 

• The temple is a masterpiece of Dravidian architecture and is called the Big Temple at Tanjore.

 

• It is made up of the vimana, ardhamandapa, mahamandapa and a large pavilion in front called the Nandimandapa.

 

• Its construction symbolises the wealth and confidence of the Chola empire at its height.

 

• The great size of the temple and the use of heavy stone blocks show the wealth the empire gathered from conquest, trade and agriculture.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The name 'Rajarajeswara' honours the king who built it.

 

• It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site as part of the Great Living Chola Temples.

 

• The vimana is the dominating feature of the structure.

 

• The temple was built mainly with granite, and its tall vimana rises in thirteen storeys, making it one of the tallest temple towers of its time.

 

NOTE

 

• Rajendra I (Option 1): Rajendra I was the son of Rajaraja I and built a Siva temple at his new capital Gangaikondacholapuram. He did not build the Tanjore Big Temple, which belongs to his father.

 

• Vijayalaya (Option 3): Vijayalaya founded the Imperial Chola line in the 9th century and reportedly captured Thanjavur, but the 1010 AD temple is a creation of the dynasty's peak, not of its founder.

 

• Rajaraja II (Option 4): Rajaraja II is credited with the Airavateswara temple at Darasuram, as the notes list. He is a later king, so he did not build the Big Temple of Tanjore.

question: The Big Temple at Tanjore is made up of several parts. Which of the following is NOT one of the parts mentioned in the notes?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Chaitya hall.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A Chaitya hall is a Buddhist prayer hall and is not part of the Big Temple; the temple consists of the vimana, ardhamandapa, mahamandapa and the Nandimandapa (चैत्य गृह — बौद्ध प्रार्थना कक्ष, मंदिर का भाग नहीं)

 

• The vimana, the tower over the sanctum, is the defining feature of a Chola temple.

 

• The Nandimandapa is the large pavilion in front that houses the bull Nandi facing the shrine of Shiva.

 

• Chaitya halls belong to the rock-cut Buddhist tradition, as at Karle, and have no place in a Dravidian Shaiva temple.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The temple was built in 1010 AD.

 

• Chola temples were mostly dedicated to Lord Shiva.

 

• The Dravidian style reached perfection under the Cholas.

 

• The temple walls also carry long inscriptions of Rajaraja I recording his conquests and the grants made for the daily needs of the shrine.

 

• A temple is the Hindu place of worship, whereas a chaitya hall and a stupa are Buddhist structures, which is a distinction examiners often use for odd-one-out questions.

 

NOTE

 

• Vimana (Option 1): The vimana is the tower above the garbhagriha and is the signature of Chola temple design, so it is part of the Big Temple. It cannot be the exception in a NOT-type question.

 

• Mahamandapa (Option 2): The mahamandapa is the large assembly hall lying in front of the sanctum and is named in the notes as a component of the Big Temple. It therefore cannot be the answer.

 

• Nandimandapa (Option 4): The Nandimandapa is the large pavilion in front housing the Nandi bull, and the notes list it as part of the temple. Because it is included, it is not the odd one out.
